hook_text: On the coast of West Africa there are doorways that millions of people walked through and never came back.
clip_script: They're called the Doors of No Return, at old forts like Elmina in Ghana and the island of Gorée in Senegal. Between the 1500s and the 1800s, more than twelve million African men, women and children were forced through doors like these onto ships bound for the Americas. Slavery already existed in West Africa, mostly of war captives, and in many places their children could become part of the community. It was not about skin colour. But the Atlantic trade changed everything: millions of people, owned forever, their children born enslaved, and slavery tied to race by racist ideas invented to excuse it. Historians count the ships. But behind every number is a person with a name and a home.
visual_style: A whiteboard stone fort on the coast with a dark doorway facing the sea; a ship on the horizon; a map with arrows from West Africa across the Atlantic; a crowd of simple figures becoming a single named silhouette.
pacing: Quiet hook, steady facts, a reflective close.
